subject: what is the definition of an interaction term between two exogenous variables?

messages.author: c72a7040a2ed8cad
messages.subject: what is the definition of an interaction term between two exogenous variables?
parts:
Hi all,

I am confused by the definition of the interaction term between two exogenous variables.
For instance, I have two exogenous variables: A and B, and their interaction C (i.e. A:B)



Then, whether C is also an exogenous variable that correlated with A and B?       
A <----> C     (i.e. C ~~ A)
B <----> C     (i.e. C ~~ B)


Or, C is an endogenous variable determined by A and B?
A ----> C      (i.e. C ~ A)
B ----> C      (i.e. C ~ B)

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: what is the definition of an interaction term between two exogenous variables?
parts:
The product AxB is determined when A and B are determined, but it is not determined by A and B.  They are jointly determined by the experimenter.  Fixed-X takes care of the situation for all, I believe.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: what is the definition of an interaction term between two exogenous variables?
parts:
I think that it is an excellent question.  This (direct effects with interaction) is not my area of expertise--I don't know what the literature says.  But, if I reason from a regression perspective, the interaction means that the effect of A and the effect of B depend on the value of the other variable.  So a generalized statement about "the effect of A" no longer makes sense.  You can now only calculate the effect of A for a certain value of B, and vice versa.  If you specify a value of B (like its mean), then you can compute simple slopes (consult a good regression text, like Cohen, Cohen, West and Aiken [2003]) and, from that, calculate the quantity that you want.  Once you get simple slopes, then you have already accounted for the interaction term.  You can plug the simple slope results into your path model and do the calculations.
     The literature may have another viw, but that's mine.
--Ed Rigdon
